strengths: The paper targets an important and practical bottleneck: inter-device communication for low-bandwidth multi-device Transformer inference. The proposed combination of sequence partitioning with vector-quantized remote token representations is intuitive and potentially useful for edge settings.

The empirical section covers several axes that matter for the proposed system, including bandwidth, device count, sequence length, compression level, and both ViT and GPT2-style models. The reported latency gains at low bandwidth are large, and the accuracy/communication trade-off tables are helpful.
The ablations on noise-augmented quantization and distributed class tokens support that these components improve accuracy relative to simpler variants, especially under aggressive compression.
The paper includes an impact/limitations discussion and honestly reports weaker zero-shot GPT2 generalization, which is an important limitation rather than something to penalize by itself.
weaknesses: The central latency claims are not fully convincing. The paper appears to benchmark a synthetic 12-layer Transformer encoder equivalent to ViT feature extraction/GPT2 input digestion, while autoregressive GPT2 decoding is said to proceed sequentially on a single device. This substantially narrows the practical significance for LLM inference, but the headline claims are framed broadly as Transformer/GPT2 inference acceleration.

The experimental methodology for latency is under-specified and possibly not representative: bandwidth is emulated, hardware details are vague, synchronization/protocol overheads are not described, and results are averaged over only 20 runs. It is unclear whether this is an implementation-level distributed system measurement or a latency model with constrained links.

The comparison to baselines has gaps. TP/SP are claimed to have no accuracy loss, but Block Parallelism/DeTransformer modifies the architecture and may affect accuracy, yet only latency is compared. The paper also does not clearly establish that baseline implementations are equally optimized or adapted to the same hardware/network setting.

The theoretical results are overstated. The Noise-Augmented VQ theorem relies on assumptions such as Gaussianity, independence, and covariance decomposition that do not generally follow from vector quantization residuals. The Distributed Class Token theorem assumes independent zero-mean quantization errors and independent class-token errors, which is not well justified given shared tokens, codebooks, and attention coupling. These proofs are better viewed as intuition than support for the general claims.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says the method is open-sourced but the URL is blank; training hyperparameters, bandwidth-emulation details, codebook initialization/update specifics, baseline implementation details, and measurement methodology are insufficient for reliable reproduction.

Presentation has several rough edges, including typos, malformed references/figure text, inconsistent terminology such as “Datasize per Token,” and some overclaiming around “comprehensive” evaluation despite using only small/medium models and limited real deployment evidence.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck: communication cost in sequence-parallel Transformer inference under low-bandwidth edge or consumer-device settings.

The core idea of transmitting vector-quantized non-local token embeddings while keeping local attention full precision is simple, plausible, and potentially useful for long-context or bandwidth-constrained inference.

The manuscript includes evaluations across vision and language models, several bandwidth/device/token-length sweeps, and ablations for noise augmentation, distributed class tokens, and commitment loss.
The limitations section honestly notes degraded zero-shot GPT generalization and increased codebook storage footprint.
weaknesses: The central deployment claim is not convincingly supported. The latency study appears to use bandwidth emulation and a 12-layer 768-dimensional encoder-like benchmark rather than a real multi-device system with realistic wireless variability, synchronization, serialization, software overheads, heterogeneous devices, or full end-to-end application pipelines.

The GPT evaluation is especially weak for the claimed inference acceleration: the method only accelerates initial prompt digestion and then autoregressive decoding proceeds on a single device. The paper does not quantify end-to-end generation latency as a function of output length, so the practical benefit for common LLM serving workloads may be far smaller than claimed.

The baseline comparisons are under-specified and potentially unfair. The paper omits accuracy for multi-device baselines by claiming they preserve the original numerical outputs, but this is not true for all listed baselines, especially architecture-modifying block-parallel methods. It is also unclear whether baseline implementations are optimized comparably or include the same system overheads.

Theoretical claims are overstated. The Wasserstein theorem is stated broadly but the proof assumes Gaussian distributions, ignores covariance between quantized embeddings and residuals when asserting covariance additivity, and later adds i.i.d. residual assumptions. The distributed class token theorem similarly relies on strong zero-mean, independence, and first-order approximations that are not justified for learned VQ errors and attention.

Accuracy results show nontrivial degradation under compression, particularly for GPT zero-shot settings, where GPT2-M perplexity increases from 43.22 to 62.29 and GPT2-S from 58.91 to 76.24 even at 32 groups. This substantially weakens claims that task performance is preserved.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The abstract says the method is open-sourced but provides no visible URL. Important details are missing, including exact bandwidth emulation method, hardware/network topology, batch size, timing methodology, codebook training details per layer, optimizer hyperparameters beyond Adam, seeds, variance/error bars, and baseline implementation details.

The communication accounting is too idealized. Reporting bits per token for VQ indices does not fully capture codebook storage, synchronization, index packing overhead, metadata, all-to-all protocol overhead, or the cost of reconstructing and projecting quantized embeddings on receiving devices.

Presentation has multiple issues that reduce confidence: typos such as 'bandwith' and 'Mpbs', inconsistent terminology, a malformed appendix/table placement, a blank open-source link, and some exaggerated phrasing such as 'real-world deployment' despite mostly simulated evidence.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and practical bottleneck: multi-device Transformer inference under low inter-device bandwidth. The motivation is clear, and the latency breakdown showing communication dominating prior methods in the 10-100 Mbps regime makes the problem compelling.

ASTRA is a coherent system design: sequence partitioning is paired with vector-quantized non-local token exchange, full-precision local attention, noise-augmented VQ training, and distributed class tokens. The method is easy to understand and the communication savings are substantial in principle.

The empirical evaluation is broader than many systems papers of this type: ViT-Base on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K, GPT2-S/M on Wikipedia and Wikitext-103, multiple bandwidths, sequence lengths, device counts, and several ablations. The reported speedups over tensor, sequence, and block parallel baselines at low bandwidth are large, and the accuracy tradeoff is acceptable for vision and fine-tuned language modeling at higher group counts.

The paper includes useful ablations for noise magnitude, distributed versus single class tokens, and commitment loss weight. These support the claim that the auxiliary design choices contribute to maintaining accuracy under aggressive compression.

The authors discuss limitations and societal considerations, including zero-shot degradation, codebook storage overhead, and robustness risks in distributed deployments. This is an appropriate and honest limitations discussion rather than a reason by itself to penalize the paper.
weaknesses: The systems evaluation is not fully convincing as evidence for real deployment. The paper says distributed inference is simulated on laptops with NVIDIA 1660Ti GPUs and bandwidth caps, but it gives limited detail about the network emulator, synchronization costs, kernel implementation, serialization overheads, startup effects, or whether the reported numbers reflect true multi-machine execution. Since the central claim is communication-efficient deployment, these details are material for soundness and reproducibility.

The latency experiments benchmark a 12-layer encoder equivalent to ViT feature extraction or GPT2 prefill, while autoregressive decoding is said to proceed sequentially on a single device. This makes the GPT-related acceleration claims somewhat narrower than the abstract and framing suggest; end-to-end generation latency, KV-cache behavior, and realistic prompt/decode mixtures are not evaluated.

Accuracy results show a nontrivial cost in some regimes, especially GPT zero-shot generalization: GPT2-M zero-shot PPL rises from 43.22 to 62.29 even with 32 groups, and GPT2-S degrades more. This is acknowledged, but it limits the method's applicability when fine-tuning on the target distribution is unavailable.

The theoretical justifications are weak relative to their formal presentation. The NAVQ Wasserstein argument relies on Gaussian and covariance assumptions that are not established for Transformer embeddings and appears to ignore possible dependence between quantized embeddings and residuals. The distributed class token proof also depends on independence, zero-mean quantization errors, and first-order softmax approximations. These results are best viewed as intuition, not strong theoretical support.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The abstract states that ASTRA is open-sourced but the URL appears missing in the extracted manuscript. Hyperparameters are only partially specified, seeds and variance/error bars are absent, bandwidth emulation details are sparse, and the baseline implementations/configurations are not sufficiently described to independently reproduce the latency comparisons.

The evaluation omits several practically relevant stress tests: heterogeneous devices, packet loss or jitter, device failure/stragglers, memory overhead from per-layer/per-group codebooks, lower precision single-device baselines such as int8/fp16 inference, and combinations with common inference optimizations. These omissions reduce confidence in how far the reported speedups will transfer.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical bottleneck: communication-dominated multi-device Transformer inference under low-bandwidth links. The motivation is compelling, especially for edge or consumer-device deployments where conventional tensor/sequence parallelism can be slower than single-device inference.

ASTRA's design is coherent: sequence partitioning plus vector-quantized transmission of non-local token representations is a natural way to reduce layer-wise all-to-all traffic, and the local-full-precision/remote-compressed attention tradeoff is well aligned with the problem.

The empirical scope is broad. The manuscript evaluates ViT, GPT2, and Llama-3-8B; reports accuracy/perplexity, communication cost, latency versus bandwidth/device count/token length, compatibility with weight quantization, heterogeneous token assignments, packet loss, dynamic bandwidth, and several ablations.

The limitations discussion is more candid than usual. It acknowledges zero-shot degradation, fine-tuning requirements, per-device-count adaptation, and that decoder-only models are accelerated only in prefill/time-to-first-token rather than full autoregressive generation.

The ablations support the main engineering choices: distributed class tokens substantially improve classification accuracy in compressed settings, noise augmentation gives a modest but consistent gain, and codebook size/group count expose a useful accuracy-latency tradeoff.
weaknesses: The systems evidence is not yet strong enough for the central deployment claims. The paper says distributed inference is simulated/emulated on laptop-class GPUs with bandwidth caps, but gives insufficient detail on the communication stack, synchronization costs, serialization/codebook lookup overheads, latency measurement protocol, warmup, batching, or whether true multi-machine wireless behavior was measured. For a communication-efficiency paper, this is a material reproducibility and soundness gap.

The headline language overstates the generative-model contribution. The abstract says ASTRA is robust on Llama-3-8B under non-ideal networks, while the main limitation later clarifies that decoder-only acceleration is only for prefill/time-to-first-token and decoding proceeds on a single device. This is useful, but much narrower than general multi-device Transformer inference or end-to-end generation acceleration.

Reproducibility is incomplete. There is no apparent code/artifact link, and the training details are sparse: optimizer is named, but key settings such as learning rates, batch sizes, schedules, hardware-specific kernels, exact model checkpoints, tokenization/preprocessing, and latency scripts are not specified sufficiently for reliable reproduction.

The theoretical results are overclaimed relative to their assumptions. The Wasserstein and distributed class token claims rely on strong Gaussian/independence/zero-mean/small-noise assumptions, and parts of the attention-error derivation treat correlated softmax perturbations as independent. These arguments are better viewed as intuition, not rigorous support for the broad claims.

Baseline comparisons raise fairness questions. Accuracy is omitted for some multi-device baselines, and the paper treats several baselines as numerically equivalent to the original model while block-parallel methods may involve architectural or training changes. The latency comparison also appears to favor communication-heavy baselines under an idealized bandwidth model without enough implementation detail.

The accuracy cost is nontrivial in some regimes. GPT2 zero-shot perplexity degrades substantially, e.g. GPT2-M from 43.22 to 62.29 even at 32 groups, and Llama downstream results show sizable drops on some tasks such as SST2 for G=1. These results temper the claim that ASTRA broadly preserves task performance under aggressive compression.

The method requires fine-tuning and separate adaptation for different device counts, which limits deployability in exactly the dynamic edge setting the paper motivates. The abstract and introduction do not make this operational cost visible enough.

Ethics and broader impact treatment is minimal in the main paper. The appendix mentions potential robustness and maintenance risks for distributed inference, but there is little discussion of failure detection, privacy/security of inter-device token exchange, or safety-critical deployment constraints.

strengths: The paper targets an important systems problem: reducing inter-device communication for multi-device Transformer inference under low-bandwidth edge-like conditions. The combination of sequence parallelism with vector-quantized remote tokens is a plausible direction with practical relevance.

The empirical section covers several axes that matter for the proposed setting, including bandwidth, device count, sequence length, compression level, vision and language tasks, and some stress tests such as packet loss and dynamic bandwidth.

The authors do include useful ablations for grouped VQ, noise magnitude, distributed class tokens, commitment loss, and codebook size, and they acknowledge some limitations such as reduced zero-shot generalization and prefill-only acceleration for decoder-only models.
weaknesses: The central latency evidence is not sufficiently convincing. The paper says deployment is simulated/emulated with bandwidth caps, but does not provide enough detail about the distributed runtime, communication stack, synchronization costs, serialization, packet behavior, or whether results are from a real multi-device implementation. Since the main claim is systems speedup at 10-100 Mbps, this missing detail is a major soundness and reproducibility problem.

The claims for generative models are overstated. ASTRA only accelerates prefill/time-to-first-token, while autoregressive decoding proceeds sequentially on a single device. This substantially narrows the significance for many LLM inference workloads, yet the abstract and main claims present broad Transformer and Llama-3-8B inference acceleration.

The theoretical results are weak and rely on assumptions that are not justified for trained Transformer embeddings. The noise-augmented VQ theorem effectively assumes Gaussian/covariance structure and independence/commutation conditions, then concludes distributional closeness in a simplified setting. The distributed class token proof assumes zero-mean, mutually independent quantization errors and independence across devices; these assumptions are unlikely to hold for deterministic VQ errors and attention outputs. Thus the theory does not strongly support the method.

The evaluation reports accuracy drops that are nontrivial for language models, especially zero-shot GPT2 where perplexity increases dramatically, e.g. GPT2-M zero-shot PPL from 43.22 to 62.29 even with 32 groups, and GPT2-S from 58.91 to 76.24. This undercuts claims that ASTRA broadly preserves task performance under compression.

Baseline comparisons are not fully satisfactory. Prior multi-device methods are treated as communication-heavy baselines, but the paper does not make clear that all baselines are implemented and optimized comparably on the same runtime/hardware. It also omits or dismisses related compression/communication baselines that could be adapted to the setting, and it compares against float32 single-device baselines in places despite modern inference commonly using lower precision.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a systems paper. The manuscript gives high-level training settings and some seeds, but no code release information, detailed runtime implementation, exact hardware/network setup, bandwidth shaping method, model adaptation details, or sufficient instructions to reproduce the latency curves and throughput experiments.

Some presentation choices make the contribution look stronger than the evidence warrants. The paper repeatedly uses large relative speedups over baselines that are extremely slow under bandwidth caps, while the more relevant absolute speedup over single-device inference is much more modest and workload-dependent. The distinction between accuracy-preserving parallelization and approximate VQ-modified inference should also be clearer.

The limitations and ethics discussion is present but uneven. The appendix impact statement discusses synchronization and safety-critical deployment concerns, but the main impact statement says no consequences need highlighting. The paper does not deeply analyze failure modes from packet loss, device failures, stale/mismatched codebooks, or robustness in safety-sensitive distributed deployments.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical bottleneck: multi-device Transformer inference under low-bandwidth links. The framing is convincing, especially the observation that existing tensor/sequence/block parallel baselines become communication dominated below roughly 100 Mbps.

ASTRA is conceptually simple and useful: keep full precision for local tokens, send vector-quantized representations for remote tokens, and add mechanisms to reduce the resulting accuracy loss. This is a plausible systems contribution with a clear latency/accuracy tradeoff knob through the number of VQ groups.

The empirical evaluation is broad. The paper reports results on ViT, GPT-2, and Llama-3-8B; vision and language tasks; varying bandwidths, device counts, and sequence lengths; heterogeneous token allocations; packet loss; dynamic bandwidth; compatibility with weight quantization; and several ablations.

The reported accuracy-latency tradeoffs are promising. For example, ViT-Base with 32 groups nearly matches the ImageNet baseline while substantially reducing communication, and Llama-3-8B prefill latency is much better than the multi-device baselines at 10-100 Mbps.

The paper discusses several meaningful limitations, including degradation in GPT zero-shot generalization, the fact that generative-model gains apply to prefill rather than full decoding, and the need for fine-tuning rather than plug-and-play deployment.
weaknesses: The theoretical claims are overstated relative to their assumptions. The proof for noise-augmented VQ relies on Gaussian/moment arguments and assumes covariance decompositions such as C_X = C_Xhat + Sigma, which need not hold because quantization residuals are generally correlated with the quantized embedding. The distributed class-token theorem similarly assumes zero-mean independent quantization errors and independent device errors, which are unlikely to hold after learned VQ and attention softmax coupling. These results are better viewed as intuition than rigorous guarantees.

The latency methodology is not sufficiently detailed for a systems paper. The manuscript says distributed inference is simulated/emulated with bandwidth caps, but does not clearly specify the communication stack, serialization overheads, synchronization costs, actual all-to-all implementation, packet retransmission behavior, or whether reported latency is measured end-to-end across physical devices. Since the central claim is communication-efficient acceleration, this weakens confidence in the headline speedups.

The baseline comparison is somewhat incomplete. TP, SP, and BP are compared mainly on latency, while the paper omits accuracy/quality tradeoffs for architectural baselines such as block parallelism. It also does not compare against potentially relevant compressed-communication or KV-cache compression variants adapted to the same setting, even if the authors argue they target different goals.

The LLM evaluation is useful but limited. ASTRA accelerates only prefill, not autoregressive decoding, so the practical gain depends strongly on workload output length. The downstream Llama task results also show nontrivial drops in some cases, e.g. SST2 for G=1 and QQP across settings, which deserves more analysis.

Reproducibility is moderate but not complete. The appendices include many settings and seed results, but no code or artifact link is provided, and several implementation details needed to reproduce latency and fine-tuning are missing or underspecified.

The method requires each participating device to maintain a full model copy plus VQ codebooks. This is acceptable for some collaborative edge settings but limits the claimed applicability to resource-constrained devices, especially for large models. The paper could discuss this deployment constraint more directly.

Some claims and wording are too strong. For example, the abstract says ASTRA remains robust on Llama-3-8B under non-ideal network conditions, but the evidence is mainly perplexity under synthetic packet loss and throughput under synthetic dynamic bandwidth traces, not a broad robustness study.
